title: Academic Writing Task 1: describing a process
status: Owner approved v1.0.0 on 2026-10-18; teacher release to all eligible schools (optional extension lesson)
rights: Original Brains Heist LLC instructional draft, AI-assisted. Process diagrams are simplified and illustrative, created for practice. Human editorial, model, mapping and originality review pending.
prerequisites: Teacher has checked actual Writing Screener and review states privately.
Optional extension: use when learners need practice with process diagrams.

objectives.text: Write a process overview that gives the number of stages, the start and the end, and any by-product.
Describe each stage in order using the present simple passive and a range of sequence devices.
Paraphrase diagram labels instead of copying them.

levels.foundation: Overview frame and sequence bank allowed and recorded; teacher reads each stage aloud before the language task.
levels.core: Write an accurate overview and body paragraph in 15 minutes with correct passives.
levels.extension: Use a "once" clause and an "after which" clause accurately.
levels.high_band: Produce a complete new 150+-word process report in 20 minutes without model, phrase bank or teacher support. Include a meaningful overview grouping stages, distinguish key transformations from minor operations, and avoid introducing unshown causes, quantities or opinions.

blocks.title: Which overview works for a process?
blocks.mode: Teacher-led analysis; learners rank before the reveal
blocks.instructions: Three learners wrote an overview for the honey diagram. Rank them, then say what is wrong with the weaker two.

examples.label: Overview A
examples.text: Overall, honey is a very healthy food that many people enjoy, and beekeeping is an important industry.
examples.comment: Off task: opinion and general knowledge are not in the diagram. An overview summarises what the diagram shows.

examples.label: Overview B
examples.text: Overall, first the hives are placed near flowers, then the bees collect nectar, and then the frames are removed.
examples.comment: Too detailed: this is the beginning of a body paragraph, not a summary of the whole process.

examples.label: Overview C
examples.text: Overall, there are eight stages in the process, beginning with the placing of hives near flowers and ending with the delivery of bottled honey to shops, with wax produced as a by-product.
examples.comment: Best: it gives the number of stages, the start and end points, and one notable feature, without detail.

blocks.title: Process language
blocks.mode: Guided practice; answer alone, then check
blocks.instructions: Look at the honey diagram. Choose the correct option, A, B or C, to complete each sentence about the process.

figure.title: How honey is produced for sale
steps: Hives are placed near flowering plants
Bees collect nectar and store it as honey
Frames full of honey are removed from the hive
Wax caps are cut off the frames
Honey is extracted by spinning the frames
Honey is filtered
Honey is stored in large tanks
Honey is bottled, labelled and sent to shops
figure.note: Simplified, illustrative process diagram for practice.
figure.alt: A process diagram with eight numbered stages. 1 Hives are placed near flowering plants. 2 Bees collect nectar and store it as honey. 3 Frames full of honey are removed from the hive. 4 Wax caps are cut off the frames; a side arrow shows the wax being made into candles. 5 Honey is extracted by spinning the frames. 6 Honey is filtered. 7 Honey is stored in large tanks. 8 Honey is bottled, labelled and sent to shops.

items.prompt: In the first stage, hives ______ near flowering plants.
items.evidence: Stage 1: Hives are placed near flowering plants
items.reason: People place the hives, so the passive is needed: are placed.

items.prompt: ______ the bees have stored enough honey, the frames are removed.
items.reason: 'Once' links the end of one stage with the start of the next.

items.prompt: The wax caps are cut off, and the wax ______ to make candles.
items.evidence: Side arrow from stage 4: wax is made into candles
items.reason: The side arrow is a by-product: it leaves the main process.

items.prompt: The honey is then extracted ______ the frames.
items.evidence: Stage 5: Honey is extracted by spinning the frames

items.prompt: After being filtered, the honey ______ in large tanks.
items.reason: 'After being filtered' is a reduced clause; the main verb is passive.

items.prompt: ______, the honey is bottled, labelled and sent to shops.
items.reason: The last stage needs an ending signpost.

blocks.support: Foundation: the teacher reads each stage aloud and asks "Who does the action? Is it important?" before learners choose.
blocks.extension: Rewrite stages 6 and 7 as one sentence using "after which".

blocks.model:
Overall, there are eight main stages in the production of honey, beginning with the placing of hives near flowering plants and ending with the delivery of bottled honey to shops. Wax is produced as a by-product of the process.

At the start of the process, beehives are positioned close to plants in flower, so that the bees can collect nectar, which they then store in the hive as honey. Once the frames inside the hive are full, they are taken out by the beekeeper. At this point, the wax caps covering the honey are cut off the frames, and this wax is used separately to make candles.

Lexical Resource: Are the stage verbs accurate, and is wording varied rather than copied from the diagram?
Grammatical Range and Accuracy: Is the present simple passive used accurately (is placed, are removed), with some complex sentences (after which, once ...)?

blocks.model:
The diagram illustrates the stages involved in producing honey for sale.

Overall, there are eight main stages in the process, beginning with the placing of hives near flowering plants and ending with the delivery of bottled honey to shops. Wax is also produced as a by-product.

At the start of the process, beehives are positioned close to plants in flower, so that the bees can collect nectar, which they then store in the hive as honey. Once the frames inside the hive are full, they are taken out by the beekeeper. At this point, the wax caps covering the honey are cut off, and this wax is used separately to make candles.

After the caps have been removed, the honey is extracted by spinning the frames, which forces the liquid out. It is then filtered to remove any remaining wax or other particles, after which it is stored in large tanks. In the final stage, the honey is put into bottles, labelled and sent to shops for sale.
checklist: Task Achievement: Is there an overview that gives the number of stages and the start and end of the process? Is every stage included, in order?
Coherence and Cohesion: Are stages grouped into logical paragraphs and linked with a range of sequence words (first, once, after this, finally)?
Lexical Resource: Are the stage verbs accurate, and is wording varied rather than copied from the diagram?
Grammatical Range and Accuracy: Is the present simple passive used accurately (is placed, are removed), with some complex sentences (after which, once ...)?

stages.title: Opening challenge: which overview works?
stages.student: Rank the three overviews before the reveal.
stages.teacher: Learners rank alone, then compare. Reveal the comments. Write the overview formula on the board: number of stages + start + end (+ one notable feature).
stages.say: A process overview tells the reader the shape of the whole process.
stages.check: Learners can name the three parts of a process overview.

stages.title: Process language
stages.teacher: Teach why the passive is normal in processes: the action matters more than who does it. Learners answer alone in 6 minutes.
stages.say: In a man-made process, use the present simple passive.

stages.title: Check process language
stages.teacher: Reveal. Collect sequence words on the board: first, once, after this, at this point, after which, finally.
stages.say: Sequence words and passives carry the reader through the process.
stages.check: Learners can use two sequence words in one sentence.

stages.title: Plan your paragraphs
stages.student: Divide the process into two groups of stages and plan your overview.
stages.teacher: Show how to split eight stages into two body paragraphs (stages 1-4 with the by-product; stages 5-8). Learners plan in note form.
stages.say: Two balanced body paragraphs make a process easy to follow.
stages.check: Each learner has a two-paragraph plan.

stages.title: Write independently
stages.student: Write the overview and the first body paragraph in 15 minutes.
stages.teacher: Time 15 minutes. Do not show the model. Record any support used.
stages.say: Change the diagram wording: do not copy each box.
stages.check: Every learner has written both paragraphs.

stages.title: Compare with the model and the criteria
stages.student: Compare your paragraphs with the model. Tick the checklist and underline your passives.
stages.teacher: Show the model. Ask learners to find three sequence devices and two verbs that are not copied from the diagram.
stages.say: The model is for discussion, not for memorising.
stages.check: Each learner has one specific improvement.

stages.title: Full Task 1 at home
stages.student: Note the homework conditions and the plan.
stages.teacher: Explain the 20-minute conditions. Learners write the start and finish times on their homework.
stages.say: Homework under real conditions shows what you can do alone.

stages.title: Exit ticket
stages.teacher: Collect exit tickets. Record the fresh-check date.
stages.say: Next time: maps and changes over time.
